passages.t: Babylon taken, and Israel seeking the LORD
passages.happening:
This is the word the LORD spoke through Jeremiah concerning Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans (verse 1). It is to be announced among the nations: Babylon is captured, Bel is put to shame, Marduk is shattered, her idols are dismayed (verse 2). A nation from the north will come against her and make her land a desolation (verse 3).

‘In those days and at that time, declares the LORD, the children of Israel and the children of Judah will come together, weeping as they come, and will seek the LORD their God’ (verse 4). ‘They will ask the way to Zion and turn their faces toward it’ (verse 5), joining themselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant. ‘My people are lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray’ (verse 6). Their enemies devoured them and said they were not guilty, for these people had sinned against the LORD (verse 7).

They are to flee from Babylon (verse 8), for God is stirring up a great alliance of nations from the north against her (verse 9). Because she rejoiced in plundering God's inheritance (verse 11), she will become a wilderness (verses 12 and 13). Israel is a scattered flock chased by lions: first the king of Assyria devoured him, and last Nebuchadnezzar gnawed his bones (verse 17). God will punish Babylon as he punished Assyria (verse 18), and bring Israel back to his pasture (verse 19). ‘A search will be made for Israel’s guilt, but there will be none’ (verse 20), for God will forgive the remnant he spares.
passages.hearers:
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II, who reigned from 605 to 562 BC, was the greatest city in the world, with vast walls, the Ishtar Gate, a great ziggurat and the temple of Marduk. Bel, meaning lord, was a title of Marduk, Babylon's chief god. The poem announces his shame.

The prophecy says a nation from the north will take Babylon; chapter 51 names the Medes. In 539 BC Babylon fell to Cyrus the Great, the Persian king who had absorbed the Median kingdom. The city was not destroyed then. It stayed an important center under the Persians and declined over the following centuries.

Verse 7 is sharp. The enemies who devoured Israel excused themselves because Israel had sinned. God answers that he will still judge them. A people's sin gives no one a license to destroy them.
passages.later: Isaiah also foretold that ‘Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms’ would be overthrown (Isaiah 13:19). Revelation takes up Babylon's fall as a picture of every proud power: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (Revelation 18:2).
passages.asks: Babylon's enemies excused their cruelty because Israel had sinned. Ask whether you have ever excused harm to someone because they deserved it. And ask what it would mean to be searched for guilt and have none found, because God has forgiven it.

passages.t: The hammer of the whole earth broken
passages.happening:
The poem calls the armies to attack Merathaim and Pekod (verse 21). There is the noise of battle in the land (verse 22). “How the hammer of the whole earth lies broken and shattered! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” (verse 23). God laid a snare for her, and she was caught (verse 24). He has opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath (verse 25).

Fugitives from Babylon declare in Zion the LORD's vengeance for his temple (verse 28). Archers are called against her, for she has been arrogant against the Holy One of Israel (verse 29). God is against her, the arrogant one (verse 31).

‘The sons of Israel are oppressed, and the sons of Judah as well’ (verse 33). Their captors will not let them go. ‘Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name. He will fervently plead their case’ (verse 34). A sword is against the Chaldeans, their wise men, false prophets, warriors, horses and treasures (verses 35 to 37). A drought is on her waters, for it is a land of idols (verse 38). Desert creatures will live there (verse 39), as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 40).

An army comes from the north, cruel and without mercy (verses 41 and 42). The king of Babylon hears and his hands go limp (verse 43). At the sound of Babylon's capture the earth will shake, and a cry will be heard among the nations (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
Babylon had been the hammer God used to strike the nations, as he had called Nebuchadnezzar his servant. Now the hammer itself is broken. The empire that broke others is judged for its own pride and cruelty.

Merathaim and Pekod are wordplays on real places. Merathaim, double rebellion, echoes a name for the marshy south of Babylonia, and Pekod, punishment, echoes the Puqudu, an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris.

The Redeemer of verse 34 is the go'el, the nearest relative who stepped in to free a kinsman. God pleads his captive people's case like a family member.

These oracles concern Babylon as an ancient empire. These notes draw no line from them to any nation, city or state of the present day.
passages.later: Isaiah also calls Israel's God ‘your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel’ (Isaiah 43:14). Proverbs says of the needy, ‘their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you’ (Proverbs 23:11).
passages.hard:
The chapter pictures Babylon destroyed and never inhabited again, but Cyrus took the city in 539 BC almost without a battle, and it stayed inhabited for centuries. Did the prophecy fail?

The difficulty is real. Readers have answered in several ways. One view reads the poem as prophetic poetry using the stock imagery of ancient curse texts and siege laments, announcing the certain end of Babylon's power in the language of total ruin; the empire did fall in 539 and never rose again, and the city's slow emptying completed the picture over time. A second view sees fulfillment in stages: the fall of the empire under Cyrus, harsher treatment of the city under later Persian kings, and its long abandonment. A third view, held by some Christian interpreters, holds that Babylon here is already becoming a symbol of proud human power, as Revelation reads it, so that the final fulfillment awaits the end of history. Some critical scholars hold that parts of the poem were written before the fall and were not fulfilled as written.

These notes set out the readings without choosing among them, and they identify no present-day power with Babylon.
passages.asks: The hammer of the whole earth was broken. Ask what power in your life seems unbreakable and is not. And ask what it means to you that your Redeemer is strong and pleads your case.
